Buttondown takes no cut of newsletter sponsorships; creators keep 100% of every sponsorship minus Stripe's processing fee
Buttondown supports over 40 integrations for embedding videos, GIFs, songs, posts, or other content
Buttondown lets users send a newsletter post directly from their personal or business email by emailing it in, and save it as a draft by sending to a different address
Buttondown charges users based on total subscriber count across all their newsletters, not by the number of newsletters created, so users can create unlimited distinct newsletters
Buttondown for Teams lets collaborators review emails before they go out, seeing drafts, suggesting changes, and helping ship with confidence

The Teams add-on costs an additional $79/month

Registered 501(c)(3) non-profits (or the equivalent in their country) get a 50% discount on their plan
Buttondown charges for active subscribers only, not all contacts
Buttondown's listed prices assume sending at most one email a day to the entire subscriber base; sending more requires contacting them about usage-based pricing
Buttondown webhooks let an external application react to events, with the documentation's own example being pointing a webhook at Slack to create a notification.
Exceeding the daily subscriber-creation cap does not return a standard rate-limit 429; instead it returns a 400 that points the caller to the imports endpoint as the supported bulk-onboarding path.
Buttondown's public API documents a POST /v1/emails endpoint that creates an email, and the sample request shows it can be created with a status implying it is sent/scheduled from code.
Creating an email via the API instantly triggers sending, based on tags and email type provided — confirming the emails endpoint composes and sends newsletter emails programmatically.
The API supports scheduling a newsletter send by setting status and publish_date on a POST to /v1/emails.
A draft email can be sent out by updating its status to 'about_to_send', at which point Buttondown automatically begins sending it.

POST /v1/subscribers is rate limited to one hundred requests per day by default, growing over time, with a contact path for higher limits, and import via CSV is suggested specifically for initial bulk import rather than ongoing volume.

assets.title: Schedule newsletters from your own code
assets.content:
Subject: Schedule newsletters from your own code
Preview text: Keep your content logic and use one documented API request to schedule delivery.

Keep your newsletter logic in your code

Hi there,

Build the newsletter in your own code, then schedule its delivery through Buttondown.

Buttondown is an email newsletter platform for creating, scheduling, and sending emails through an API. Your code stays in charge of how the content comes together.

When your script is ready, authenticate with a Buttondown API token and post the email to `/v1/emails`. Add `status: scheduled` and a future `publish_date` to set the send time.

API access, including scheduling, is available on the free plan. Buttondown handles the scheduled newsletter send after your own code prepares and submits the request.

The official documentation shows the request in Python, Ruby, JavaScript, and cURL, so you can see whether it fits the workflow you want to run.

See the scheduling request → https://docs.buttondown.com/scheduling-emails-via-the-api

- Buttondown

asset_metadata.single_idea: Buttondown can take a newsletter produced by the reader’s own code and schedule its send through a documented API request, with API access available on the free plan.

selected_brief.selection_reason: This audience wants control over how newsletter content is assembled and includes budget-conscious operators. The documented scheduling API gives them a concrete way to connect their own logic to newsletter delivery, while free-plan API access lowers the commercial barrier without becoming the main proposition.

value_case.reader_benefit: If the reader assembles newsletters in their own code, they can keep that logic there and use Buttondown’s API to schedule the resulting newsletter email for delivery.
value_case.mechanism: A script authenticates with a Buttondown API token and posts an email to /v1/emails with its status and publish_date set for the scheduled send.
decision_conditions: The reader must supply and run the code that prepares and submits the request.
Requests require a Buttondown API token.
API access, including API scheduling, is available on the free plan.

claim_conditions: Authenticate the API request with a Buttondown token.
Set the email’s status and publish_date to schedule it.
The reader remains responsible for the external automation logic and trigger.
Authenticate requests with a Buttondown API token in the Authorization header (R12).
Set the email's status and publish_date fields to schedule a send, or update a draft's status to 'about_to_send' to dispatch it (R14, R15).
Create a webhook for the specific event and point its URL at your own application to react to Buttondown events (R6).
Use the CSV-file imports endpoint for bulk subscriber loads rather than per-subscriber POSTs (R10).

The stated mechanism is an API, and it is documented for drafting, scheduling, sending and subscriber creation, but the named tools have no documented native connectors — those links depend on generic API, webhook or Zapier use (R7, R6) — and programmatic subscriber creation is capped at 100/day by default with CSV import as the documented bulk path (R16, R10).

Problem P1 is an inferred audience hypothesis: On a tight hobby-project budget, the vendor's built-in newsletter automation (RSS-to-email) sits above what the operator can pay for, so they fall back to the API tier and write their own automation logic instead. Use it only conditionally (if this is relevant to the reader), not as a known current pain, behavior or outcome of the recipient. Product fit does not establish current demand or a demonstrated customer outcome.
Historical sources (2023-10-02); present applicability is not corroborated.
Single-source problem; independent corroboration is not established.

The selected evidence establishes that the API and API scheduling are available on all plans including free and that the first 100 subscribers cost nothing, but it does not establish the price of the built-in RSS-to-email automation the operator rejected, nor remove the need to write the automation logic.
selected_brief.job: Get the reader to inspect Buttondown’s documented scheduling request and decide whether it fits the newsletter workflow they want to control in code.
selected_brief.single_idea: Buttondown can take a newsletter produced by the reader’s own code and schedule its send through a documented API request, with API access available on the free plan.
selected_brief.felt_need: On a tight hobby-project budget, the vendor's built-in newsletter automation (RSS-to-email) sits above what the operator can pay for, so they fall back to the API tier and write their own automation logic instead.
selected_brief.mechanism: Buttondown documents POST /v1/emails for creating an email. Supplying status and publish_date schedules the send; the request authenticates with an API token.

alternative_arguments.selection_reason: For a developer-minded operator, being able to retrieve newsletter content in ordinary file formats is a distinct reason to consider the platform. The public export documentation answers that control question before adoption.

value_case.reader_benefit: The operator can retrieve their Buttondown email records and message contents as files they can inspect and store outside the dashboard.
value_case.mechanism: Starting an email export from the Emails tab downloads a CSV and a folder containing each email’s contents as Markdown files.
decision_conditions: The export is initiated from the Emails tab in the Buttondown dashboard.
The documented mechanism covers email content; it does not establish a complete export of every kind of account or engagement data.

claim_conditions: Describe the output specifically as a CSV plus email contents in Markdown files.
Do not characterize the export as self-hosting, legal ownership, or a complete platform backup.

Set the email's status and publish_date fields to schedule a send, or update a draft's status to 'about_to_send' to dispatch it (R14, R15).
Create a webhook for the specific event and point its URL at your own application to react to Buttondown events (R6).
Use the CSV-file imports endpoint for bulk subscriber loads rather than per-subscriber POSTs (R10).

The stated mechanism is an API, and it is documented for drafting, scheduling, sending and subscriber creation, but the named tools have no documented native connectors — those links depend on generic API, webhook or Zapier use (R7, R6) — and programmatic subscriber creation is capped at 100/day by default with CSV import as the documented bulk path (R16, R10).
alternative_arguments.single_idea: Buttondown provides a documented way to download email data as a CSV and each email’s contents as Markdown files.
alternative_arguments.mechanism: From the Emails tab, the operator initiates an export that downloads a CSV and a folder of Markdown files containing the emails.
alternative_arguments.belief_shift: Before: adopting a newsletter platform may mean leaving published email content accessible only through its interface. After: Buttondown documents a file-based email export whose exact contents can be inspected before adoption.
must_not_say: That the export proves outright ownership of the archive.
That it is a complete backup of subscribers, engagement data, consent records, settings, or the entire account.
That exported content becomes independently hosted.
That the export guarantees an easy or lossless migration to another provider.
alternative_arguments.objection: If I publish my newsletter there, can I retrieve the email content in ordinary files?
alternative_arguments.next_step_decision: Decide whether the documented CSV-and-Markdown export provides acceptable access to newsletter email content.
alternative_arguments.next_step_value: The official page documents this verified fact: Buttondown documents an email export mechanism that downloads a CSV plus a folder containing the contents of each email as Markdown files.
alternative_arguments.next_step_limit: The page does not establish legal ownership, retention rights, a complete account backup, or export coverage for subscriber engagement and consent data.
alternative_arguments.subject_strategy: Lead with the concrete CSV-and-Markdown export rather than broad claims about ownership, portability, or avoiding lock-in.

selected_brief.belief_shift: Before: Buttondown may appear to require operating a newsletter primarily through its interface or paid automation features. After: the reader sees a documented API route for scheduling a newsletter produced by their own code, available on the free plan.
must_not_say: That Buttondown writes, hosts, or triggers the reader’s external automation logic.
That the workflow eliminates the need to run code or maintain whatever environment executes it.
That Buttondown provides native CRM, Slack, GitHub, or Google Sheets connectors for this workflow.
That API scheduling resolves complaints about dense documentation.
That the API is unlimited, faster, easier, or more reliable than alternatives.
That a specific recipient currently uses scripts, spreadsheets, GitHub Actions, Google Apps Script, or any other named stack.
That the built-in RSS-to-email automation has any current price not established by the licensed evidence.
That Buttondown will save a quantified amount of time or produce subscriber, engagement, or revenue gains.
Named customer adoption, testimonials, case studies, or comparative superiority.
Subscriber-import limits, sponsorships, paid subscriptions, teams, attachments, custom domains, privacy claims, and other unrelated features.
Do not state or imply that every reader uses Scheduling. Present this integration conditionally (for example, 'If you use Scheduling...') unless the user-supplied campaign context establishes it.
Do not state or imply that every reader uses Create. Present this integration conditionally (for example, 'If you use Create...') unless the user-supplied campaign context establishes it.

reader_verdicts.what_it_sells: Buttondown is a newsletter platform whose API lets my code submit an email now and schedule Buttondown to send it later, potentially removing a manual send step from my week.
reader_verdicts.relevance_feedback: The profile explicitly establishes only that I am a developer-minded newsletter operator. Running newsletter content and sending from my own code is inferred from observed market context, not established as my workflow. The email addresses that workflow directly and conditionally enough to be plausible, but whether I currently have a script or need scheduled API delivery remains unknown.
assumed_experiences: Email-only: I build or want to build newsletter content in my own code.

Email-only: handing scheduled delivery to Buttondown would improve my workflow.

reader_verdicts.problem_now: Scheduled delivery from code is relevant to the kind of workflow I could plausibly run, and the free-plan claim lowers the barrier to investigating it. reader_verdicts.to_click_it_would_have_to: I would have clicked if this email had told me the main free-plan limits that apply to scheduled API sends; the precise endpoint and low-effort documentation CTA are enough for me to click anyway.

brief.interpretation: I interpret “introduce our product to a new buyer” as a single acquisition email for a prospective developer-minded newsletter operator, not onboarding for an existing customer. The email should introduce Buttondown through one concrete use case—scheduling newsletter sends from the reader’s own code—and ask them to inspect the public implementation documentation.
brief.reader:
Selected audience: Developer-minded newsletter operator.
Research context describes some members of this market, not this recipient's installed tools or experiences. Follow the campaign request when it scopes the job.
Observed situation (inferred; check applicability): A hobby-project or small-team operator runs a newsletter on Buttondown but drives the content and sending from their own code and spreadsheets rather than Buttondown's web UI, writing Google Apps Script against the Buttondown API to pull RSS feeds and post emails, and tolerating a manual trigger step because their requirements never specified fully automatic sending.
brief.promise: Buttondown can serve as the sending layer behind a newsletter workflow the reader controls in code: its API can schedule newsletter emails, and API access is available on the free plan.
brief.orientation: Buttondown is an email newsletter platform that lets developer-minded operators create, schedule, and send newsletter emails through an API.
brief.arc: In one email, move the reader from seeing Buttondown as another newsletter interface to understanding one concrete, documented use: scheduling a newsletter send from their own code, then inspecting the exact mechanism before signing up.
brief.sequence_rationale: A single-email acquisition campaign needs one complete reason to want Buttondown, not a catalogue. API scheduling is the strongest fit for this solution-aware audience: it supports control over newsletter assembly, has a concrete implementation mechanism, and is available on the free plan. The public scheduling documentation is the appropriate first step because it lets a developer inspect the request and conditions before creating an account. No customer proof is used because the licensed campaign boundary does not establish any named customer or outcome claim. Which customers or quotes may we name?

emails.selection_reason: This audience wants control over how newsletter content is assembled and includes budget-conscious operators. The documented scheduling API gives them a concrete way to connect their own logic to newsletter delivery, while free-plan API access lowers the commercial barrier without becoming the main proposition.

value_case.reader_benefit: If the reader assembles newsletters in their own code, they can keep that logic there and use Buttondown’s API to schedule the resulting newsletter email for delivery.
value_case.mechanism: A script authenticates with a Buttondown API token and posts an email to /v1/emails with its status and publish_date set for the scheduled send.
decision_conditions: The reader must supply and run the code that prepares and submits the request.
Requests require a Buttondown API token.
API access, including API scheduling, is available on the free plan.

claim_conditions: Authenticate the API request with a Buttondown token.
Set the email’s status and publish_date to schedule it.
The reader remains responsible for the external automation logic and trigger.
Authenticate requests with a Buttondown API token in the Authorization header (R12).
Set the email's status and publish_date fields to schedule a send, or update a draft's status to 'about_to_send' to dispatch it (R14, R15).
Create a webhook for the specific event and point its URL at your own application to react to Buttondown events (R6).
Use the CSV-file imports endpoint for bulk subscriber loads rather than per-subscriber POSTs (R10).

The stated mechanism is an API, and it is documented for drafting, scheduling, sending and subscriber creation, but the named tools have no documented native connectors — those links depend on generic API, webhook or Zapier use (R7, R6) — and programmatic subscriber creation is capped at 100/day by default with CSV import as the documented bulk path (R16, R10).

Problem P1 is an inferred audience hypothesis: On a tight hobby-project budget, the vendor's built-in newsletter automation (RSS-to-email) sits above what the operator can pay for, so they fall back to the API tier and write their own automation logic instead. Use it only conditionally (if this is relevant to the reader), not as a known current pain, behavior or outcome of the recipient. Product fit does not establish current demand or a demonstrated customer outcome.
Historical sources (2023-10-02); present applicability is not corroborated.
Single-source problem; independent corroboration is not established.

The selected evidence establishes that the API and API scheduling are available on all plans including free and that the first 100 subscribers cost nothing, but it does not establish the price of the built-in RSS-to-email automation the operator rejected, nor remove the need to write the automation logic.

alternative_arguments.selection_reason: For a developer-minded operator, being able to retrieve newsletter content in ordinary file formats is a distinct reason to consider the platform. The public export documentation answers that control question before adoption.

decision_conditions: The export is initiated from the Emails tab in the Buttondown dashboard.
The documented mechanism covers email content; it does not establish a complete export of every kind of account or engagement data.

claim_conditions: Describe the output specifically as a CSV plus email contents in Markdown files.

alternative_arguments.single_idea: Buttondown provides a documented way to download email data as a CSV and each email’s contents as Markdown files.
alternative_arguments.mechanism: From the Emails tab, the operator initiates an export that downloads a CSV and a folder of Markdown files containing the emails.
alternative_arguments.belief_shift: Before: adopting a newsletter platform may mean leaving published email content accessible only through its interface. After: Buttondown documents a file-based email export whose exact contents can be inspected before adoption.
must_not_say: That the export proves outright ownership of the archive.
That it is a complete backup of subscribers, engagement data, consent records, settings, or the entire account.
That exported content becomes independently hosted.
That the export guarantees an easy or lossless migration to another provider.
alternative_arguments.objection: If I publish my newsletter there, can I retrieve the email content in ordinary files?
alternative_arguments.next_step_decision: Decide whether the documented CSV-and-Markdown export provides acceptable access to newsletter email content.
alternative_arguments.next_step_value: The official page documents this verified fact: Buttondown documents an email export mechanism that downloads a CSV plus a folder containing the contents of each email as Markdown files.
alternative_arguments.next_step_limit: The page does not establish legal ownership, retention rights, a complete account backup, or export coverage for subscriber engagement and consent data.
alternative_arguments.subject_strategy: Lead with the concrete CSV-and-Markdown export rather than broad claims about ownership, portability, or avoiding lock-in.

That the workflow eliminates the need to run code or maintain whatever environment executes it.
That Buttondown provides native CRM, Slack, GitHub, or Google Sheets connectors for this workflow.
That API scheduling resolves complaints about dense documentation.
That the API is unlimited, faster, easier, or more reliable than alternatives.

allowed_claims: The API is available on all plans, including the free plan

Buttondown will migrate a user's mailing list to Buttondown for free, regardless of list size, via a concierge migration service
Buttondown does not charge extra for paid subscribers on its paid subscriptions feature, letting creators keep all revenue they make
Buttondown is GDPR-compliant and does not collect any data about users or their subscribers by default
Buttondown takes no cut of newsletter sponsorships; creators keep 100% of every sponsorship minus Stripe's processing fee
Buttondown supports over 40 integrations for embedding videos, GIFs, songs, posts, or other content
Buttondown lets users send a newsletter post directly from their personal or business email by emailing it in, and save it as a draft by sending to a different address
Buttondown charges users based on total subscriber count across all their newsletters, not by the number of newsletters created, so users can create unlimited distinct newsletters
Buttondown for Teams lets collaborators review emails before they go out, seeing drafts, suggesting changes, and helping ship with confidence
Teams access control lets you give an editor access to drafts but not billing, and let a marketing lead manage subscribers without touching API keys
Buttondown is free for the first 100 subscribers
The Teams add-on costs an additional $79/month
The Email attachments add-on costs an additional $9/month
Registered 501(c)(3) non-profits (or the equivalent in their country) get a 50% discount on their plan
Buttondown charges for active subscribers only, not all contacts
Buttondown's listed prices assume sending at most one email a day to the entire subscriber base; sending more requires contacting them about usage-based pricing
Buttondown webhooks let an external application react to events, with the documentation's own example being pointing a webhook at Slack to create a notification.
Exceeding the daily subscriber-creation cap does not return a standard rate-limit 429; instead it returns a 400 that points the caller to the imports endpoint as the supported bulk-onboarding path.
Buttondown's public API documents a POST /v1/emails endpoint that creates an email, and the sample request shows it can be created with a status implying it is sent/scheduled from code.
Creating an email via the API instantly triggers sending, based on tags and email type provided — confirming the emails endpoint composes and sends newsletter emails programmatically.
The API supports scheduling a newsletter send by setting status and publish_date on a POST to /v1/emails.
A draft email can be sent out by updating its status to 'about_to_send', at which point Buttondown automatically begins sending it.

POST /v1/subscribers is rate limited to one hundred requests per day by default, growing over time, with a contact path for higher limits, and import via CSV is suggested specifically for initial bulk import rather than ongoing volume.

partial_caveats_injected: Authenticate requests with a Buttondown API token in the Authorization header (R12).
Set the email's status and publish_date fields to schedule a send, or update a draft's status to 'about_to_send' to dispatch it (R14, R15).

Use the CSV-file imports endpoint for bulk subscriber loads rather than per-subscriber POSTs (R10).
